memory_update.text: LRN is the cleanest US-listed direct exposure to K-12 virtual schooling and career learning because its revenue is materially tied to virtual/blended public-school services and Career Learning.
PSO is the second cleanest large-cap direct exposure through Connections Academy/Pearson Virtual Schools and a growing CTE/career-readiness credential stack.
NRDY is a below-$1B exception because Varsity Tutors directly targets K-12 tutoring, district intervention, and AI-enhanced live instruction.

The likely chokepoint for this node is not curriculum alone; it is the combination of state/district authorization, recurring public funding, school operations, parent trust, teacher capacity, and demonstrable student outcomes.

Several strong node-relevant businesses appear private or nonprofit and are therefore not direct US-listed candidates in this pass: Imagine Learning/Edgenuity, Edmentum, HMH, Apex Learning, Renaissance, NWEA, Cambium, Amplify, Khan Academy, and many state-run virtual schools.

LRN is the highest-purity US-listed candidate for the K-12 virtual schooling and career-pathway node because it combines virtual school operations, long-duration school-as-a-service contracts, curriculum, LMS, support services, and middle/high-school career pathways.
PSO is a second direct operator/supplier through Pearson Virtual Learning and Connections Academy, but exposure is diluted by the broader Pearson portfolio.

The apparent chokepoint is public authorization plus durable school/district contracts and outcomes credibility; digital curriculum alone is less scarce because many curriculum vendors are private, nonprofit, or commoditized.
TYL and GOOGL are infrastructure mappings, not pure plays: they support K-12 administrative and device/platform capacity, but stock-level sensitivity to this node may be low.

Important private or nonprofit competitors/suppliers remain outside the US-listed universe: PowerSchool/Instructure status needs re-checking after privatization activity, and major K-12 assessment/curriculum entities such as College Board, ETS, NWEA, Curriculum Associates, Renaissance, HMH, Infinite Campus, and Edmentum are not clean US-listed public equities.

Need a later pass on regulated funding and policy risk: charter authorizers, state virtual-school caps, attendance rules, tutoring funding after pandemic-relief rolloff, and evidence standards for high-dosage tutoring could be the true gating variables.
LRN is the direct pure-play anchor for the k12_virtual_career_pathways node: virtual/blended public schools plus General Education and Career Learning school-as-a-service.
PSO is a diversified but important virtual-school competitor/supplier through Pearson Virtual Schools and Connections Academy; isolate Virtual Learning economics before ranking.
NRDY is a direct tutoring/remediation candidate but below USD 1B and exposed to district/federal/state funding delays; include as high-relevance, high-risk exception.
COUR may be an underappreciated career-pathways/credential supplier for high schools, but current evidence is case-study level rather than disclosed K-12 revenue scale.
KLTR is a second-order virtual-classroom infrastructure supplier; include only as a supplier hypothesis until K-12 customer concentration or named district/operator relationships are verified.

Many important K-12 assessment/curriculum/tutoring vendors are private or recently taken private, including PowerSchool, Renaissance, IXL, Edmentum, Newsela, and HMH; public-market coverage is therefore incomplete.

For this node, the key chokepoint appears to be public-sector authorization, charter/district contract durability, funding continuity, and outcomes credibility rather than generic digital curriculum supply.

summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the US-listed universe for the K-12 virtual schooling, tutoring/intervention, digital curriculum, and career-pathway node. The most direct public exposures found are Stride and Pearson, both operating K-12 virtual school platforms with public-school or district relationships. Smaller-cap direct exposure exists through Nerdy/Varsity Tutors in online tutoring and intervention. Scholastic and Graham Holdings/Kaplan are included as adjacent public suppliers or platform owners tied to K-12 curriculum, school solutions, pre-college, and career exploration, but their chokepoint exposure is less pure than Stride/Pearson. Several highly relevant operators in credit recovery, virtual curriculum, and assessments appear private or nonprofit, creating a public-market coverage gap. Expanded the US-listed universe around the K-12 virtual schooling and career-pathway node, emphasizing scarce or durable inputs: public-sector authorization, long-duration school-as-a-service contracts, virtual-school operating capacity, LMS/SIS/ERP infrastructure, managed student devices, tutoring/intervention capacity, and credibility around measurable outcomes. This is research support only and contains no buy/sell recommendation. Expanded universe for the K-12 virtual schooling and career-pathway node. The clearest direct public-market mappings are Stride and Pearson through full-time virtual public-school operations and K-12 virtual-school platforms. Less obvious second-order or adjacent candidates include Nerdy for district-facing high-dosage tutoring, Coursera for high-school career credentials
